The study used a dataset of 150 JET plasmas with approximately 8 minutes of steady-state plasma and 15,000 ELMs.
The Beryllium II (527nm) radiation signal was used to identify ELMs.
ELM energies are independent of waiting times beyond 0.02 seconds.
The ELM waiting time probability density function (pdf) shows a series of maxima and zeros at approximately 0.08 second intervals.
The average energy of ELMs in the first large group is roughly 60% of the ELMs in later groups.
The 10 millisecond timescale is consistent with a resistive relaxation of the plasma's edge.
The study found that ELM energies are not inversely proportional to waiting time.
The JET plasmas used in the study had approximately 12 MW of NBI heating.
The fuelling rate of the JET plasmas was 1.4 x 10^22 Ds^-1.
The effective charge (Z_eff) of the JET plasmas was 1.2.
The triangularity (δ) of the JET plasmas was 0.2.
The plasmas had approximately 6 seconds of steady H-mode, with 2.3 seconds of exceptionally steady plasma between 11.5 and 13.8 seconds.
The line-integrated plasma density and thermal energy were used as measures of the density and energy losses associated with ELMs.
The study found that the line-integrated plasma density and thermal energy have two timescales: 0.005 seconds and 0.01 seconds.
The 0.005 second timescale is consistent with a rapid rise in heat flux, while the 0.01 second timescale is consistent with a slower transport process.
The study found that the thermal plasma energy relaxes to a minimum on a timescale of 10 milliseconds after an ELM.
